article.title: Case Study: Tourism New Zealand website

items.sentence_raw: New Zealand is a small country of four million inhabitants, a long-haul flight from all the major tourist-generating markets of the world.
Tourism currently makes up 9% of the country's gross domestic product, and is the country's largest export sector.
Unlike other export sectors, which make products and then sell them overseas, tourism brings its customers to New Zealand.
The product is the country itself - the people, the places and the experiences.
In 1999, Tourism New Zealand launched a campaign to communicate a new brand position to the world.
The campaign focused on New Zealand's scenic beauty, exhilarating outdoor activities and authentic Maori culture, and it made New Zealand one of the strongest national brands in the world.
A key feature of the campaign was the website www.newzealand.com, which provided potential visitors to New Zealand with a single gateway to everything the destination had to offer.
The heart of the website was a database of tourism services operators, both those based in New Zealand and those based abroad which offered tourism services to the country.
Any tourism-related business could be listed by filling in a simple form.
This meant that even the smallest bed and breakfast address or specialist activity provider could gain a web presence with access to an audience of long-haul visitors.
In addition, because participating businesses were able to update the details they gave on a regular basis, the information provided remained accurate.
items.explain: Q1: The passage says businesses were able to *'update the details they gave on a regular basis'*. The question asks what businesses could do to information regularly — **'update'** is the exact word from the passage. So the answer is **update**.

items.sentence_raw: And to maintain and improve standards, Tourism New Zealand organised a scheme whereby organisations appearing on the website underwent an independent evaluation against a set of agreed national standards of quality.
As part of this, the effect of each business on the environment was considered.
items.explain: Q2: The passage says *'the effect of each business on the environment was considered'*. The question asks about the evaluation including impact on the **environment** — **'effect'** here means **'impact'**. So the answer is **environment**.

items.sentence_raw: To communicate the New Zealand experience, the site also carried features relating to famous people and places.
One of the most popular was an interview with former New Zealand All Blacks rugby captain Tana Umaga.
items.explain: Q3: The passage mentions an interview with *'former New Zealand All Blacks rugby captain Tana Umaga'*. The question asks for a former sports **captain** — **'rugby'** is a sport, and **'captain'** is his role. So the answer is **captain**.

items.sentence_raw: Another feature that attracted a lot of attention was an interactive journey through a number of the locations chosen for blockbuster films which had made use of New Zealand's stunning scenery as a backdrop.
items.explain: Q4: The passage describes *'an interactive journey through a number of the locations chosen for blockbuster films'*. The question asks about locations used in **films** — **'blockbuster films'** means big, popular movies. So the answer is **films**.

items.sentence_raw: As the site developed, additional features were added to help independent travellers devise their own customised itineraries.

To make it easier to plan motoring holidays, the site catalogued the most popular driving routes in the country, highlighting different routes according to the season and indicating distances and times.
items.explain: Q5: The passage says driving routes were highlighted *'according to the season'*. The question says information varied depending on the **season** — **'according to'** means **'depending on'**. So the answer is **season**.

items.sentence_raw: Later, a Travel Planner feature was added, which allowed visitors to click and 'bookmark' places or attractions they were interested in, and then view the results on a map.
The Travel Planner offered suggested routes and public transport options between the chosen locations.
There were also links to accommodation in the area.
items.explain: Q6: The passage says *'There were also links to accommodation in the area'*. The question asks about details of local **accommodation** — **'links to'** means the website provided this information. So the answer is **accommodation**.

items.sentence_raw: By registering with the website, users could save their Travel Plan and return to it later, or print it out to take on the visit.
The website also had a 'Your Words' section where anyone could submit a blog of their New Zealand travels for possible inclusion on the website.
items.explain: Q7: The passage says anyone could *'submit a blog of their New Zealand travels'*. The question asks what travellers could send a link to — they could send a link to their **blog**. So the answer is **blog**.

items.sentence_raw: The Tourism New Zealand website won two Webby awards for online achievement and innovation.
More importantly perhaps, the growth of tourism to New Zealand was impressive.
Overall tourism expenditure increased by an average of 6.9% per year between 1999 and 2004.
From Britain, visits to New Zealand grew at an average annual rate of 13% between 2002 and 2006, compared to a rate of 4% overall for British visits abroad.
The website was set up to allow both individuals and travel organisations to create itineraries and travel packages to suit their own needs and interests.
items.explain: Q8: The passage says the website allowed people to *'create itineraries and travel packages to suit their own needs'* — this means they make their **own** plans. The question says the website aimed to provide **'ready-made'** plans — ***'create your own' is the opposite of 'ready-made'***. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: On the website, visitors can search for activities not solely by geographical location, but also by the particular nature of the activity.

This is important as research shows that activities are the key driver of visitor satisfaction, contributing 74% to visitor satisfaction, while transport and accommodation account for the remaining 26%.
items.explain: Q10: The passage says activities contribute *'74% to visitor satisfaction'*, while *'transport and accommodation account for the remaining 26%'*. The question says 26% is related to **accommodation alone** — but the passage says 26% is for **both** transport and accommodation together. ***The passage combines them, the question separates them*** — so the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: The more activities that visitors undertake, the more satisfied they will be.
It has also been found that visitors enjoy cultural activities most when they are interactive, such as visiting a marae (meeting ground) to learn about traditional Maori life.
items.explain: Q11: The passage says visitors enjoy cultural activities most when they are *'interactive, such as visiting a marae to learn about traditional Maori life'*. The question says visitors like to **'become involved'** in local culture — **'interactive'** and **'become involved'** mean the same thing. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: Many long-haul travellers enjoy such learning experiences, which provide them with stories to take home to their friends and family.
In addition, it appears that visitors to New Zealand don't want to be 'one of the crowd' and find activities that involve only a few people more special and meaningful.
It could be argued that New Zealand is not a typical destination.
New Zealand is a small country with a visitor economy composed mainly of small businesses.
It is generally perceived as a safe English-speaking country with a reliable transport infrastructure.
Because of the long-haul flight, most visitors stay for longer (average 20 days) and want to see as much of the country as possible on what is often seen as a once-in-a-lifetime visit.
items.explain: Q13: The passage says a visit to New Zealand is *'often seen as a once-in-a-lifetime visit'*. The question says visitors feel it is **unlikely they will return** — **'once-in-a-lifetime'** means you do it only one time, so you probably will not come back. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: However, the underlying lessons apply anywhere - the effectiveness of a strong brand, a strategy based on unique experiences and a comprehensive and user-friendly website.

The question asks about what most visitors did first, but this information is simply missing. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.

The question asks about a preference for small hotels, but this specific comparison is missing. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.

article.title: Why being bored is stimulating - and useful, too

items.sentence_raw: We all know how it feels - it's impossible to keep your mind on anything, time stretches out, and all the things you could do seem equally unlikely to make you feel better.
But defining boredom so that it can be studied in the lab has proved difficult.
items.explain: Q14: The passage says *'defining boredom so that it can be studied in the lab has proved difficult'* — this shows a **problem** with the **scientific approach**. The heading **iv** (*'Problems with a scientific approach to boredom'*) matches this exactly. So the answer is **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: For a start, it can include a lot of other mental states, such as frustration, apathy, depression and indifference.
There isn't even agreement over whether boredom is always a low-energy, flat kind of emotion or whether feeling agitated and restless counts as boredom, too.
In his book, Boredom: A Lively History, Peter Toohey at the University of Calgary, Canada, compares it to disgust - an emotion that motivates us to stay away from certain situations.
"If disgust protects humans from infection, boredom may protect them from 'infectious' social situations," he suggests.
items.explain: Q20: The passage says boredom *'may protect them from 'infectious' social situations'* — **'protect from'** means **'avoid an unpleasant experience'**. This matches idea **E** (*'Boredom may encourage us to avoid an unpleasant experience'*). So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: By asking people about their experiences of boredom, Thomas Goetz and his team at the University of Konstanz in Germany have recently identified five distinct types: indifferent, calibrating, searching, reactant and apathetic.
items.explain: Q15: The passage says Goetz *'identified five distinct types'* of boredom — this is a **system of classification**. The heading **vi** (*'Creating a system of classification for feelings of boredom'*) matches this. So the answer is **vi**.

items.sentence_raw: These can be plotted on two axes - one running left to right, which measures low to high arousal, and the other from top to bottom, which measures how positive or negative the feeling is.
Intriguingly, Goetz has found that while people experience all kinds of boredom, they tend to specialise in one.
Of the five types, the most damaging is 'reactant' boredom with its explosive combination of high arousal and negative emotion.
items.explain: Q21: The passage says *'the most damaging is 'reactant' boredom'* — **'most damaging'** means **'worse than all the others'**. This matches idea **B** (*'One sort of boredom is worse than all the others'*). So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The most useful is what Goetz calls 'indifferent' boredom: someone isn't engaged in anything satisfying but still feels relaxed and calm.
However, it remains to be seen whether there are any character traits that predict the kind of boredom each of us might be prone to.
Psychologist Sandi Mann at the University of Central Lancashire, UK, goes further.
"All emotions are there for a reason, including boredom," she says.
Mann has found that being bored makes us more creative.
items.explain: Q16: The passage says *'being bored makes us more creative'* — **'creative'** means producing new ideas, which is a **productive outcome**. The heading **i** (*'The productive outcomes that may result from boredom'*) matches this. So the answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: "We're all afraid of being bored but in actual fact it can lead to all kinds of amazing things," she says.

In experiments published last year, Mann found that people who had been made to feel bored by copying numbers out of the phone book for 15 minutes came up with more creative ideas about how to use a polystyrene cup than a control group.
Mann concluded that a passive, boring activity is best for creativity because it allows the mind to wander.
In fact, she goes so far as to suggest that we should seek out more boredom in our lives.
Psychologist John Eastwood at York University in Toronto, Canada, isn't convinced.
"If you are in a state of mind-wandering you are not bored," he says.
"In my view, by definition boredom is an undesirable state."
That doesn't necessarily mean that it isn't adaptive, he adds.
"Pain is adaptive - if we didn't have physical pain, bad things would happen to us.
Does that mean that we should actively cause pain?
No.
But even if boredom has evolved to help us survive, it can still be toxic if allowed to fester."
For Eastwood, the central feature of boredom is a failure to put our 'attention system' into gear.
This causes an inability to focus on anything, which makes time seem to go painfully slowly.
items.explain: Q24: The passage says boredom causes *'an inability to focus on anything'* — **'inability to focus'** means people **cannot focus**. So the answer is **focus**.

items.sentence_raw: What's more, your efforts to improve the situation can end up making you feel worse.
items.explain: Q22: The passage says *'your efforts to improve the situation can end up making you feel worse'* — **'efforts to improve'** means **'trying to cope'**, and **'making you feel worse'** means **'increase its negative effects'**. This matches idea **D** (*'Trying to cope with boredom can increase its negative effects'*). So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: "People try to connect with the world and if they are not successful there's that frustration and irritability," he says.
Perhaps most worryingly, says Eastwood, repeatedly failing to engage attention can lead to a state where we don't know what to do any more, and no longer care.
Eastwood's team is now trying to explore why the attention system fails.
It's early days
but they think that at least some of it comes down to personality.
Boredom proneness has been linked with a variety of traits.
People who are motivated by pleasure seem to suffer particularly badly.
items.explain: Q25: The passage says *'People who are motivated by pleasure seem to suffer particularly badly'* — **'motivated by pleasure'** means **pleasure** is an important aim. So the answer is **pleasure**.

items.sentence_raw: Other personality traits, such as curiosity, are associated with a high boredom threshold.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says *'personality traits, such as curiosity, are associated with a high boredom threshold'* — a **'high boredom threshold'** means you can **cope with it**. So the answer is **curiosity**.

items.sentence_raw: More evidence that boredom has detrimental effects comes from studies of people who are more or less prone to boredom.
It seems those who bore easily face poorer prospects in education, their career and even life in general.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says *'those who bore easily face poorer prospects'* — this means we can **identify** people who are **most affected** by boredom. The heading **viii** (*'Identifying those most affected by boredom'*) matches this. So the answer is **viii**.

items.sentence_raw: But of course, boredom itself cannot kill - it's the things we do to deal with it that may put us in danger.
items.explain: Q17: The passage says *'the things we do to deal with it may put us in danger'* — this is a **potential danger** from how we react to boredom. The heading **v** (*'A potential danger arising from boredom'*) matches this. So the answer is **v**.

items.sentence_raw: What can we do to alleviate it before it comes to that?
Goetz's group has one suggestion.

Working with teenagers, they found that those who 'approach' a boring situation - in other words, see that it's boring and get stuck in anyway - report less boredom than those who try to avoid it by using snacks, TV or social media for distraction.
Psychologist Francoise Wemelsfelder speculates that our over-connected lifestyles might even be a new source of boredom.
items.explain:
Q19: The passage says our *'over-connected lifestyles'* are a *'new source of boredom'* — this is a **new explanation**. It also says we should *'use boredom to motivate us'* — this is a **new cure**. The heading **iii** (*'A new explanation and a new cure for boredom'*) matches both. So the answer is **iii**.

Q23: The passage says our *'over-connected lifestyles might even be a new source of boredom'* — **'over-connected lifestyles'** means **'the way we live today'**. This matches idea **A** (*'The way we live today may encourage boredom'*). So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: "In modern human society there is a lot of overstimulation but still a lot of problems finding meaning," she says.
So instead of seeking yet more mental stimulation, perhaps we should leave our phones alone, and use boredom to motivate us to engage with the world in a more meaningful way.
items.explain: Q19: The passage says our *'over-connected lifestyles'* are a *'new source of boredom'* — this is a **new explanation**. It also says we should *'use boredom to motivate us'* — this is a **new cure**. The heading **iii** (*'A new explanation and a new cure for boredom'*) matches both. So the answer is **iii**.

article.title: Artificial artists

items.sentence_raw: The Painting Fool is one of a growing number of computer programs which, so their makers claim, possess creative talents.
items.explain: Q27: The first paragraph lists big successes: *'Classical music... had audiences enraptured'*, *'Artworks... sold for thousands'*, and *'software... creates art that could not have been imagined'*. All these examples show that **a great deal of progress** has already happened. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Classical music by an artificial composer has had audiences enraptured, and even tricked them into believing a human was behind the score.
items.explain: Q27: The first paragraph lists big successes: *'Classical music... had audiences enraptured'*, *'Artworks... sold for thousands'*, and *'software... creates art that could not have been imagined'*. All these examples show that **a great deal of progress** has already happened. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Artworks painted by a robot have sold for thousands of dollars and been hung in prestigious galleries.
items.explain: Q27: The first paragraph lists big successes: *'Classical music... had audiences enraptured'*, *'Artworks... sold for thousands'*, and *'software... creates art that could not have been imagined'*. All these examples show that **a great deal of progress** has already happened. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: And software has been built which creates art that could not have been imagined by the programmer.
Human beings are the only species to perform sophisticated creative acts regularly.
If we can break this process down into computer code, where does that leave human creativity?
"This is a question at the very core of humanity," says Geraint Wiggins, a computational creativity researcher at Goldsmiths, University of London.
"It scares a lot of people.
They are worried that it is taking something special away from what it means to be human."
items.explain: Q28: Wiggins says people are scared because *'it is taking something special away from what it means to be human'*. **'Something special'** about being human is a **fundamental human quality** — like creativity. So the worry is that computer art **undermines** this quality, making the answer **C**.

items.sentence_raw: To some extent, we are all familiar with computerised art.
The question is: where does the work of the artist stop and the creativity of the computer begin?
Consider one of the oldest machine artists, Aaron, a robot that has had paintings exhibited in London's Tate Modern and the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art.
Aaron can pick up a paintbrush and paint on canvas on its own.
Impressive perhaps, but it is still little more than a tool to realise the programmer's own creative ideas.
Simon Colton, the designer of the Painting Fool, is keen to make sure his creation doesn't attract the same criticism.
Unlike earlier 'artists' such as Aaron, the Painting Fool only needs minimal direction and can come up with its own concepts by going online for material.
items.explain: Q29: The key difference is about where ideas come from. The passage says *'Unlike earlier 'artists' such as Aaron, the Painting Fool... can come up with its own concepts by going online for material'*. So Aaron depends on the programmer, but the Painting Fool finds its own **source of subject matter**. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: The software runs its own web searches and trawls through social media sites.
It is now beginning to display a kind of imagination too, creating pictures from scratch.
One of its original works is a series of fuzzy landscapes, depicting trees and sky.
While some might say they have a mechanical look, Colton argues that such reactions arise from people's double standards towards software-produced and human-produced art.
items.explain: Q30: Colton argues that negative reactions *'arise from people's double standards towards software-produced and human-produced art'*. **'Double standards'** means judging by **different criteria** — being stricter with computers than with humans. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: After all, he says, consider that the Painting Fool painted the landscapes without referring to a photo.
"If a child painted a new scene from its head, you'd say it has a certain level of imagination," he points out.
"The same should be true of a machine."
Software bugs can also lead to unexpected results.
Some of the Painting Fool's paintings of a chair came out in black and white, thanks to a technical glitch.
This gives the work an eerie, ghostlike quality.
items.explain: Q31: The chair paintings resulted from a *'technical glitch'*, but the passage says *'This gives the work an eerie, ghostlike quality'*. **'Eerie, ghostlike'** is a **particularly striking effect**, not a failure. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Human artists like the renowned Ellsworth Kelly are lauded for limiting their colour palette - so why should computers be any different?
Researchers like Colton don't believe it is right to measure machine creativity directly to that of humans who 'have had millennia to develop our skills'.
items.explain: Q32: Colton says it is not right to measure machine creativity directly to humans who *'have had millennia to develop our skills'*. This means we should avoid **comparing** human and computer artistic achievements right now. So the correct ending is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Others, though, are fascinated by the prospect that a computer might create something as original and subtle as our best artists.
So far, only one has come close.
Composer David Cope invented a program called Experiments in Musical Intelligence, or EMI.
Not only did EMI create compositions in Cope's style, but also that of the most revered classical composers, including Bach, Chopin and Mozart.
items.explain: Q33: EMI *'fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach'*. **'Fooled'** means the music was **virtually indistinguishable** from a human's work. So the correct ending is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Audiences were moved to tears, and EMI even fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach.
items.explain: Q33: EMI *'fooled classical music experts into thinking they were hearing genuine Bach'*. **'Fooled'** means the music was **virtually indistinguishable** from a human's work. So the correct ending is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Not everyone was impressed however.
Some, such as Wiggins, have blasted Cope's work as pseudoscience, and condemned him for his deliberately vague explanation of how the software worked.
items.explain: Q34: Wiggins *'condemned him for his deliberately vague explanation of how the software worked'*. A **'vague explanation'** means he was **not revealing the technical details**. So the correct ending is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: Meanwhile, Douglas Hofstadter of Indiana University said EMI created replicas which still rely completely on the original artist's creative impulses.
items.explain: Q35: Hofstadter said EMI created *'replicas which still rely completely on the original artist's creative impulses'*. This means the work was **entirely dependent on the imagination of its creator**, not the computer's. So the correct ending is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: When audiences found out the truth they were often outraged with Cope, and one music lover even tried to punch him.
items.explain: Q36: The passage says *'When audiences found out the truth they were often outraged'*. **'Found out the truth'** means **discovering it was the product of a computer program**. So the correct ending is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: Amid such controversy, Cope destroyed EMI's vital databases.
But why did so many people love the music, yet recoil when they discovered how it was composed?
items.explain: Q38: The passage asks why people *'recoil when they discovered how it was composed'*, then says Moffat's study *'provides a clue'*. A **'clue'** means it helps **explain** the reaction. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: A study by computer scientist David Moffat of Glasgow Caledonian University provides a clue.
items.explain: Q38: The passage asks why people *'recoil when they discovered how it was composed'*, then says Moffat's study *'provides a clue'*. A **'clue'** means it helps **explain** the reaction. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: He asked both expert musicians and non-experts to assess six compositions.
The participants weren't told beforehand whether the tunes were composed by humans or computers, but were asked to guess, and then rate how much they liked each one.
items.explain: Q37: The participants *'weren't told beforehand whether the tunes were composed by humans or computers'*. This means they had to assess the music **without knowing** its source. So the correct ending is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: People who thought the composer was a computer tended to dislike the piece more than those who believed it was human.
This was true even among the experts, who might have been expected to be more objective in their analyses.
Where does this prejudice come from?
Paul Bloom of Yale University has a suggestion: he reckons part of the pleasure we get from art stems from the creative process behind the work.

items.sentence_raw: Most often, however, the spice found its primary use as an additive to food and drink.

items.sentence_raw: The spice then travelled from that great trading city to markets all around Europe.

Because the overland trade route allowed for only small quantities of the spice to reach Europe, and because Venice had a virtual monopoly of the trade, the Venetians could set the price of cinnamon exorbitantly high.
These prices, coupled with the increasing demand, spurred the search for new routes to Asia by Europeans eager to take part in the spice trade.
Seeking the high profits promised by the cinnamon market, Portuguese traders arrived on the island of Ceylon in the Indian Ocean toward the end of the 15th century.
Before Europeans arrived on the island, the state had organized the cultivation of cinnamon.
People belonging to the ethnic group called the Salagama would peel the bark off young shoots of the cinnamon plant in the rainy season, when the wet bark was more pliable.
During the peeling process, they curled the bark into the 'stick' shape still associated with the spice today.

When the Portuguese arrived, they needed to increase production significantly, and so enslaved many other members of the Ceylonese native population, forcing them to work in cinnamon harvesting.

items.explain: Q10: The passage says the Portuguese built a fort in 1518 and developed a monopoly, and the Dutch only broke this *'150-year Portuguese monopoly'* in 1640 — so the Portuguese had control throughout the 16th century. The answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: In the late 16th century, for example, they enjoyed a tenfold profit when shipping cinnamon over a journey of eight days from Ceylon to India.

article.title: Oxytocin

items.sentence_raw: Oxytocin is a chemical, a hormone produced in the pituitary gland in the brain.
It was through various studies focusing on animals that scientists first became aware of the influence of oxytocin.
items.explain: Q21: The passage says the earliest findings came from *'various studies focusing on animals'*. So the answer is **animals**.

items.sentence_raw: They discovered that it helps reinforce the bonds between prairie voles, which mate for life, and triggers the motherly behaviour that sheep show towards their newborn lambs.
It is also released by women in childbirth, strengthening the attachment between mother and baby.
items.explain: Q22: The passage directly states oxytocin is *'released by women in childbirth'*. So the answer is **childbirth**.

items.sentence_raw: Few chemicals have as positive a reputation as oxytocin, which is sometimes referred to as the 'love hormone'.
One sniff of it can, it is claimed, make a person more trusting, empathetic, generous and cooperative.
It is time, however, to revise this wholly optimistic view.
A new wave of studies has shown that its effects vary greatly depending on the person and the circumstances, and it can impact on our social interactions for worse as well as for better.
Oxytocin's role in human behaviour first emerged in 2005.

In a groundbreaking experiment, Markus Heinrichs and his colleagues at the University of Freiburg, Germany, asked volunteers to do an activity in which they could invest money with an anonymous person who was not guaranteed to be honest.
The team found that participants who had sniffed oxytocin via a nasal spray beforehand invested more money than those who received a placebo instead.
items.explain:
Q18: The finding is that people are **more trusting**. The passage describes an experiment where people who sniffed oxytocin *'invested more money'* with an anonymous person — investing money with a stranger shows **trust**. This experiment was done by **Markus Heinrichs**, so the answer is **A**.

Q23: The 2005 experiment gave participants oxytocin or a *'placebo'* — a **placebo** is a substance with no effect, used for comparison. So the answer is **placebo**.

items.sentence_raw: The study was the start of research into the effects of oxytocin on human interactions.
"For eight years, it was quite a lonesome field," Heinrichs recalls.
items.explain: Q16: The question asks about a period with **little scientific attention**. The passage quotes a researcher saying, *'For eight years, it was quite a lonesome field'* — **'lonesome'** here means few people were studying it. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: "Now, everyone is interested."
These follow-up studies have shown that after a sniff of the hormone, people become more charitable, better at reading emotions on others' faces and at communicating constructively in arguments.
items.explain: Q14: You might look for the word *'beneficial'*, but the passage uses different words. The passage says oxytocin makes people *'more charitable, better at reading emotions... and at communicating constructively'* — these are all **beneficial effects**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Together, the results fuelled the view that oxytocin universally enhanced the positive aspects of our social nature.
Then, after a few years, contrasting findings began to emerge.

Simone Shamay-Tsoory at the University of Haifa, Israel, found that when volunteers played a competitive game, those who inhaled the hormone showed more pleasure when they beat other players, and felt more envy when others won.
items.explain:
Q19: The finding is about increased **jealousy**. The passage says that in a competitive game, people on oxytocin *'felt more envy when others won'* — **'envy'** is a direct match for **'jealousy'**. This study was by **Simone Shamay-Tsoory**, so the answer is **B**.

Q24: The Haifa study had participants take part in a *'competitive game'* which revealed negative emotions. So the answer is **game**.

items.sentence_raw: What's more, administering oxytocin also has sharply contrasting outcomes depending on a person's disposition.
items.explain: Q20: The finding is that the effect **varies from one type of person to another**. The passage says oxytocin has *'sharply contrasting outcomes depending on a person's disposition'* — **'disposition'** means the type of person. This was found by **Jennifer Bartz**, so the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Jennifer Bartz from Mount Sinai School of Medicine, New York, found that it improves people's ability to read emotions, but only if they are not very socially adept to begin with.
Her research also shows that oxytocin in fact reduces cooperation in subjects who are particularly anxious or sensitive to rejection.
Another discovery is that oxytocin's effects vary depending on who we are interacting with.

Studies conducted by Carolyn DeClerck of the University of Antwerp, Belgium, revealed that people who had received a dose of oxytocin actually became less cooperative when dealing with complete strangers.
items.explain: Q25: The Antwerp study showed people became *'less cooperative when dealing with complete strangers'*. A lack of willingness to help means less cooperation, so the answer is **strangers**.

items.sentence_raw: Meanwhile, Carsten De Dreu at the University of Amsterdam in the Netherlands discovered that volunteers given oxytocin showed favouritism: Dutch men became quicker to associate positive words with Dutch names than with foreign ones, for example.
items.explain: Q26: The Amsterdam study found people quicker to associate positive words with *'Dutch names'* than foreign ones. So the familiar things with positive associations are **names**.

items.sentence_raw: According to De Dreu, oxytocin drives people to care for those in their social circles and defend them from outside dangers.
So, it appears that oxytocin strengthens biases, rather than promoting general goodwill, as was previously thought.
There were signs of these subtleties from the start.
Bartz has recently shown that in almost half of the existing research results, oxytocin influenced only certain individuals or in certain circumstances.
Where once researchers took no notice of such findings, now a more nuanced understanding of oxytocin's effects is propelling investigations down new lines.
items.explain: Q17: The question says people were **ignoring certain aspects of their research data**. The passage states that *'once researchers took no notice of such findings'* — **'took no notice'** is a direct match for **'ignoring'**. So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: To Bartz, the key to understanding what the hormone does lies in pinpointing its core function rather than in cataloguing its seemingly endless effects.
There are several hypotheses which are not mutually exclusive.
Oxytocin could help to reduce anxiety and fear.
Or it could simply motivate people to seek out social connections.

She believes that oxytocin acts as a chemical spotlight that shines on social clues - a shift in posture, a flicker of the eyes, a dip in the voice - making people more attuned to their social environment.
This would explain why it makes us more likely to look others in the eye and improves our ability to identify emotions.
But it could also make things worse for people who are overly sensitive or prone to interpreting social cues in the worst light.
Perhaps we should not be surprised that the oxytocin story has become more perplexing.
The hormone is found in everything from octopuses to sheep, and its evolutionary roots stretch back half a billion years.
"It's a very simple and ancient molecule that has been co-opted for many different functions," says Sue Carter at the University of Illinois, Chicago, USA.
"It affects primitive parts of the brain like the amygdala, so it's going to have many effects on just about everything."
Bartz agrees.

"Oxytocin probably does some very basic things, but once you add our higher-order thinking and social situations, these basic processes could manifest in different ways depending on individual differences and context."
items.explain: Q15: The question asks for **reasons** why effects are complex. The passage explains that oxytocin does *'very basic things'*, but when you add *'higher-order thinking and social situations'*, these basics *'manifest in different ways depending on individual differences and context'*. This directly gives the reasons for the complexity, so the answer is **F**.

article.title: MAKING THE MOST OF TRENDS

items.sentence_raw: Most managers can identify the major trends of the day.

But in the course of conducting research in a number of industries and working directly with companies, we have discovered that managers often fail to recognize the less obvious but profound ways these trends are influencing consumers' aspirations, attitudes, and behaviors.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says managers *'often fail to recognize the less obvious but profound ways these trends are influencing consumers'* — **'less obvious but profound ways'** means the big, hidden impact. The question says managers *'are unaware of the significant impact'* — **'unaware'** matches **'fail to recognize'**, and **'significant impact'** matches **'profound ways'**. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: This is especially true of trends that managers view as peripheral to their core markets.
Many ignore trends in their innovation strategies or adopt a wait-and-see approach and let competitors take the lead.
At a minimum, such responses mean missed profit opportunities.
At the extreme, they can jeopardize a company by ceding to rivals the opportunity to transform the industry.

The purpose of this article is twofold: to spur managers to think more expansively about how trends could engender new value propositions in their core markets, and to provide some high-level advice on how to make market research and product development personnel more adept at analyzing and exploiting trends.

One strategy, known as 'infuse and augment', is to design a product or service that retains most of the attributes and functions of existing products in the category but adds others that address the needs and desires unleashed by a major trend.
A case in point is the Poppy range of handbags, which the firm Coach created in response to the economic downturn of 2008.
The Coach brand had been a symbol of opulence and luxury for nearly 70 years, and the most obvious reaction to the downturn would have been to lower prices.
However, that would have risked cheapening the brand's image.
items.explain: Q28: The passage says lowering prices *'would have risked cheapening the brand's image'* — **'cheapening the brand's image'** means hurting its luxury reputation. The question says Coach was anxious to *'safeguard its reputation as a manufacturer of luxury goods'* — **'safeguard'** means protect, which matches avoiding the risk. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Instead, they initiated a consumer-research project which revealed that customers were eager to lift themselves and the country out of tough times.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says Coach's research *'revealed that customers were eager to lift themselves and the country out of tough times'* — **'eager to lift themselves out of tough times'** means a positive attitude towards difficult circumstances. The statement says *'customers had a positive attitude towards dealing with difficult circumstances'* — **'positive attitude'** matches **'eager'**, and **'difficult circumstances'** matches **'tough times'**. So the answer is **A (Coach)**.

items.sentence_raw: Using these insights, Coach launched the lower-priced Poppy handbags, which were in vibrant colors, and looked more youthful and playful than conventional Coach products.
Creating the sub-brand allowed Coach to avert an across-the-board price cut.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says *'Creating the sub-brand allowed Coach to avert an across-the-board price cut'* — **'avert an across-the-board price cut'** means successfully avoided charging less for its core products. The statement says *'successfully avoided having to charge its customers less for its core products'* — **'avoided'** matches **'avert'**, and **'charge less'** matches **'price cut'**. So the answer is **A (Coach)**.

items.sentence_raw: In contrast to the many companies that responded to the recession by cutting prices, Coach saw the new consumer mindset as an opportunity for innovation and renewal.
A further example of this strategy was supermarket Tesco's response to consumers' growing concerns about the environment.
items.explain: Q36: The passage says Tesco responded to *'consumers' growing concerns about the environment'* — this is a **lifestyle trend** in an area unrelated to retail products. The statement says *'responded to a growing lifestyle trend in an unrelated product sector'* — **'lifestyle trend'** matches **'concerns about the environment'**, and **'unrelated product sector'** means the trend was not about retail itself. So the answer is **C (Nike)**.

items.sentence_raw: With that in mind, Tesco, one of the world's top five retailers, introduced its Greener Living program, which demonstrates the company's commitment to protecting the environment by involving consumers in ways that produce tangible results.
For example, Tesco customers can accumulate points for such activities as reusing bags, recycling cans and printer cartridges, and buying home-insulation materials.
items.explain: Q34: The passage says *'Tesco customers can accumulate points for such activities as reusing bags, recycling cans'* — this is an **incentive scheme** to reward green actions. The statement says *'implemented an incentive scheme to demonstrate its corporate social responsibility'* — **'incentive scheme'** matches the points system, and **'corporate social responsibility'** matches the environmental focus. So the answer is **B (Tesco)**.

items.sentence_raw: Like points earned on regular purchases, these green points can be redeemed for cash.
Tesco has not abandoned its traditional retail offerings but augmented its business with these innovations, thereby infusing its value proposition with a green streak.
items.explain: Q29: The passage says *'Tesco has not abandoned its traditional retail offerings but augmented its business'* — **'not abandoned'** means it kept its core activities the same. The question says the programme *'did not require Tesco to modify its core business activities'* — **'modify'** means change, and the passage confirms no change was needed. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: A more radical strategy is 'combine and transcend'.

This entails combining aspects of the product's existing value proposition with attributes addressing changes arising from a trend, to create a novel experience - one that may land the company in an entirely new market space.
At first glance, spending resources to incorporate elements of a seemingly irrelevant trend into one's core offerings sounds like it's hardly worthwhile.
items.explain: Q30: The passage says *'spending resources to incorporate elements of a seemingly irrelevant trend into one's core offerings sounds like it's hardly worthwhile'* — **'hardly worthwhile'** means it seems to have few benefits. The question says the strategy *'might appear to have few obvious benefits'* — **'appear'** matches **'sounds like'**, and **'few obvious benefits'** matches **'hardly worthwhile'**. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: But consider Nike's move to integrate the digital revolution into its reputation for high-performance athletic footwear.

In 2006, they teamed up with technology company Apple to launch Nike+, a digital sports kit comprising a sensor that attaches to the running shoe and a wireless receiver that connects to the user's iPod.
items.explain: Q33: The passage says Nike *'teamed up with technology company Apple to launch Nike+'* — **'teamed up'** means collaborated with another manufacturer. The statement says *'extended its offering by collaborating with another manufacturer'* — **'collaborating'** matches **'teamed up'**, and **'another manufacturer'** is Apple. So the answer is **C (Nike)**.

items.sentence_raw: By combining Nike's original value proposition for amateur athletes with one for digital consumers, the Nike+ sports kit and web interface moved the company from a focus on athletic apparel to a new plane of engagement with its customers.

A third approach, known as 'counteract and reaffirm', involves developing products or services that stress the values traditionally associated with the category in ways that allow consumers to oppose - or at least temporarily escape from - the aspects of trends they view as undesirable.
A product that accomplished this is the ME2, a video game created by Canada's iToys.
By reaffirming the toy category's association with physical play, the ME2 counteracted some of the widely perceived negative impacts of digital gaming devices.
Like other handheld games, the device featured a host of exciting interactive games, a full-color LCD screen, and advanced 3D graphics.

What set it apart was that it incorporated the traditional physical component of children's play: it contained a pedometer, which tracked and awarded points for physical activity (walking, running, biking, skateboarding, climbing stairs).
The child could use the points to enhance various virtual skills needed for the video game.
The ME2, introduced in mid-2008, catered to kids' huge desire to play video games while countering the negatives, such as associations with lack of exercise and obesity.
items.explain:
Q31: The passage says the ME2 *'catered to kids' huge desire to play video games while countering the negatives, such as associations with lack of exercise and obesity'* — **'countering the negatives'** means it addressed unhealthy lifestyle concerns. The question says it *'addressed people's concerns about unhealthy lifestyles'* — **'addressed'** matches **'countering'**, and **'unhealthy lifestyles'** matches **'lack of exercise and obesity'**. So the answer is **D**.

Q32: The passage says the ME2 *'countered some of the widely perceived negative impacts of digital gaming devices'* — **'negative impacts'** means harmful effects. items.sentence_raw: For millennia, the coconut has been central to the lives of Polynesian and Asian peoples.
In the western world, on the other hand, coconuts have always been exotic and unusual, sometimes rare.

Today, images of palm-fringed tropical beaches are cliches in the west to sell holidays, chocolate bars, fizzy drinks and even romance.

The leaves have hard veins in their centres which, in many parts of the world, are used as brushes after the green part of the leaf has been stripped away.
Immature coconut flowers are tightly clustered together among the leaves at the top of the trunk.
The flower stems may be tapped for their sap to produce a drink, and the sap can also be reduced by boiling to produce a type of sugar used for cooking.
items.explain: Q2: The passage says the sap can be *'reduced by boiling to produce a type of sugar used for cooking'* — so the sap becomes a source of **sugar**. The answer is **sugar**.

items.sentence_raw: Coconut palms produce as many as seventy fruits per year, weighing more than a kilogram each.
The wall of the fruit has three layers: a waterproof outer layer, a fibrous middle layer and a hard, inner layer.
The thick fibrous middle layer produces coconut fibre, 'coir', which has numerous uses and is particularly important in manufacturing ropes.
items.explain: Q3: The passage says the middle layer is *'particularly important in manufacturing ropes'* — so it is used for **ropes**. The answer is **ropes**.

items.sentence_raw: The woody innermost layer, the shell, with its three prominent 'eyes', surrounds the seed.
An important product obtained from the shell is charcoal, which is widely used in various industries as well as in the home as a cooking fuel.
items.explain: Q4: The passage says *'an important product obtained from the shell is charcoal'* — so the shell is a source of **charcoal**. The answer is **charcoal**.

items.sentence_raw: When broken in half, the shells are also used as bowls in many parts of Asia.
items.explain: Q5: The passage says *'when broken in half, the shells are also used as bowls'* — so halved shells become **bowls**. The answer is **bowls**.

items.sentence_raw: Inside the shell are the nutrients (endosperm) needed by the developing seed.
Initially, the endosperm is a sweetish liquid, coconut water, which is enjoyed as a drink, but also provides the hormones which encourage other plants to grow more rapidly and produce higher yields.

items.sentence_raw: As the fruit matures, the coconut water gradually solidifies to form the brilliant white, fat-rich, edible flesh or meat.

items.sentence_raw: A derivative of coconut fat, glycerine, acquired strategic importance in a quite different sphere, as Alfred Nobel introduced the world to his nitroglycerine-based invention: dynamite.
items.explain: Q8: The passage says glycerine from coconut fat led to *'Alfred Nobel introduced... his nitroglycerine-based invention: dynamite'* — so glycerine is an ingredient in **dynamite**. The answer is **dynamite**.

items.sentence_raw: Their biology would appear to make coconuts the great maritime voyagers and coastal colonizers of the plant world.

items.sentence_raw: The air pocket in the seed, created as the endosperm solidifies, protects the embryo.

There have been centuries of academic debate over the origins of the coconut.

16th century trade and human migration patterns reveal that Arab traders and European sailors are likely to have moved coconuts from South and Southeast Asia to Africa and then across the Atlantic to the east coast of America.

items.sentence_raw: But the origin of coconuts discovered along the west coast of America by 16th century sailors has been the subject of centuries of discussion.

items.sentence_raw: In America, there are close coconut relatives, but no evidence that coconuts are indigenous.

items.sentence_raw: The typical way of talking to a baby - high-pitched, exaggerated and repetitious - is a source of fascination for linguists who hope to understand how 'baby talk' impacts on learning.

items.sentence_raw: Some research even suggests that infants are listening to adult speech as early as 10 weeks before being born, gathering the basic building blocks of their family's native tongue.

items.sentence_raw: They played repeating vowel sounds made by a special synthesizing device that mimicked sounds made by either an adult woman or another baby.
This way, only the impact of the auditory cues was observed.

items.sentence_raw: The Harappan Civilisation of ancient Pakistan and India flourished 5,000 years ago, but a thousand years later their cities were abandoned.

article.title: Cutty Sark: the fastest sailing ship of all time

items.sentence_raw: The nineteenth century was a period of great technological development in Britain, and for shipping the major changes were from wind to steam power, and from wood to iron and steel.
The fastest commercial sailing vessels of all time were clippers, three-masted ships built to transport goods around the world, although some also took passengers.
items.explain: Q1: The passage says clippers were *'built to transport goods'*, and *'some also took passengers'* — this means passengers were extra, not the main purpose. The question says they were ***originally intended*** for passengers, which is the opposite. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: From the 1840s until 1869, when the Suez Canal opened and steam propulsion was replacing sail, clippers dominated world trade.
Although many were built, only one has survived more or less intact: Cutty Sark, now on display in Greenwich, southeast London.
Cutty Sark's unusual name comes from the poem "Tam O'Shanter" by the Scottish poet Robert Bums.
items.explain: Q2: The passage says the name comes from a *'poem'*, but the question says it is the name of a *'character'* — ***a poem is not a character***. The name actually comes from a *'short nightdress'* in the poem, not a person. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Tam, a farmer, is chased by a witch called Nannie, who is wearing a 'cutty sark' - an old Scottish name for a short nightdress.
The witch is depicted in Cutty Sark's figurehead - the carving of a woman typically at the front of old sailing ships.
In legend, and in Burns's poem, witches cannot cross water, so this was a rather strange choice of name for a ship.
Cutty Sark was built in Dumbarton, Scotland, in 1869, for a shipping company owned by John Willis.
To carry out construction, Willis chose a new shipbuilding firm, Scott & Linton, and ensured that the contract with them put him in a very strong position.
items.explain: Q3: The passage says the contract *'put him in a very strong position'* — **'strong position'** means it **favoured** Willis. The question says the contract **favoured Willis**, which matches exactly. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: In the end, the firm was forced out of business, and the ship was finished by a competitor.

Willis's company was active in the tea trade between China and Britain, where speed could bring shipowners both profits and prestige, so Cutty Sark was designed to make the journey more quickly than any other ship.
items.explain: Q4: The passage says Cutty Sark was *'designed to make the journey more quickly than any other ship'* — **'more quickly than any other'** means **the fastest**. The question says Willis wanted it to be the **fastest** tea clipper, which is the same idea. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: On her maiden voyage, in 1870, she set sail from London, carrying large amounts of goods to China.
She returned laden with tea, making the journey back to London in four months.
However, Cutty Sark never lived up to the high expectations of her owner, as a result of bad winds and various misfortunes.
On one occasion, in 1872, the ship and a rival clipper, "Thermopylae", left port in China on the same day.
Crossing the Indian Ocean, Cutty Sark gained a lead of over 400 miles, but then her rudder was severely damaged in stormy seas, making her impossible to steer.
The ship's crew had the daunting task of repairing the rudder at sea, and only succeeded at the second attempt.
Cutty Sark reached London a week after "Thermopylae".
items.explain: Q5: The passage says Cutty Sark *'reached London a week after Thermopylae'* — **'after'** means it was slower, not faster. The question says Cutty Sark **beat** Thermopylae, which means it arrived first. These are opposites, so the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Steam ships posed a growing threat to clippers, as their speed and cargo capacity increased.
In addition, the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, the same year that Cutty Sark was launched, had a serious impact.

While steam ships could make use of the quick, direct route between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea, the canal was of no use to sailing ships, which needed the much stronger winds of the oceans, and so had to sail a far greater distance.
Steam ships reduced the journey time between Britain and China by approximately two months.
items.explain: Q6: The passage says steam ships *'reduced the journey time between Britain and China by approximately two months'* — **'reduced journey time'** means they were **faster**. The question says steam ships could travel **faster** than clippers, which matches. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: By 1878, tea traders weren't interested in Cutty Sark, and instead, she took on the much less prestigious work of carrying any cargo between any two ports in the world.
In 1880, violence aboard the ship led ultimately to the replacement of the captain with an incompetent drunkard who stole the crew's wages.
He was suspended from service, and a new captain appointed.
This marked a turnaround and the beginning of the most successful period in Cutty Sark's working life, transporting wool from Australia to Britain.
items.explain: Q9: The passage says the most successful period involved *'transporting wool from Australia to Britain'* — **'transporting'** means it was the main **cargo**. So the answer is **wool**.

items.sentence_raw: One such journey took just under 12 weeks, beating every other ship sailing that year by around a month.
The ship's next captain, Richard Woodget, was an excellent navigator, who got the best out of both his ship and his crew.
items.explain: Q10: The passage says Woodget was *'an excellent navigator'* — **'excellent'** means he was very **skilled**. The question asks for his role besides captain, and **'navigator'** is that role. So the answer is **navigator**.

items.sentence_raw: As a sailing ship, Cutty Sark depended on the strong trade winds of the southern hemisphere, and Woodget took her further south than any previous captain, bringing her dangerously close to icebergs off the southern tip of South America.
items.explain: Q8: The passage says Woodget brought the ship *'dangerously close to icebergs'* — **'dangerously close'** means there was a **risk of hitting** one. The question says he put it **at risk of hitting an iceberg**, which is the same idea. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: His gamble paid off, though, and the ship was the fastest vessel in the wool trade for ten years.
As competition from steam ships increased in the 1890s, and Cutty Sark approached the end of her life expectancy, she became less profitable.
She was sold to a Portuguese firm, which renamed her "Ferreira".
For the next 25 years, she again carried miscellaneous cargoes around the world.
Badly damaged in a gale in 1922, she was put into Falmouth harbour in southwest England, for repairs.
items.explain: Q11: The passage says the ship was *'badly damaged in a gale'* and then went to Falmouth for repairs — **'gale'** is a strong storm that caused the damage. So the answer is **gale**.

items.sentence_raw: Wilfred Dowman, a retired sea captain who owned a training vessel, recognised her and tried to buy her, but without success.
She returned to Portugal and was sold to another Portuguese company.
Dowman was determined, however, and offered a high price: this was accepted, and the ship returned to Falmouth the following year and had her original name restored.
Dowman used Cutty Sark as a training ship, and she continued in this role after his death.
items.explain: Q12: The passage says Dowman *'used Cutty Sark as a training ship'* and this continued until 1954 — **'used as'** means its purpose was **training**. So the answer is **training**.

items.sentence_raw: When she was no longer required, in 1954, she was transferred to dry dock at Greenwich to go on public display.
The ship suffered from fire in 2007, and again, less seriously, in 2014, but now Cutty Sark attracts a quarter of a million visitors a year.
items.explain: Q13: The passage says the ship *'suffered from fire in 2007, and again... in 2014'* — **'suffered from'** means it was **damaged by** fire twice. So the answer is **fire**.

orphan_explain_map.7: Q7: The passage says steam ships used the *'quick, direct route'* through the Suez Canal, and sailing ships needed the *'ocean'* route. But the passage never says if steam ships ***sometimes*** used the ocean route too. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.

article.title: SAVING THE SOIL
glossary: * Humus: the part of the soil formed from dead plant material

items.sentence_raw: More than a third of the world's soil is endangered, according to a recent UN report.
If we don't slow the decline, all farmable soil could be gone in 60 years.
Since soil grows 95% of our food, and sustains human life in other more surprising ways, that is a huge problem.
Peter Groffman, from the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies in New York, points out that soil scientists have been warning about the degradation of the world's soil for decades.
At the same time, our understanding of its importance to humans has grown.
A single gram of healthy soil might contain 100 million bacteria, as well as other microorganisms such as viruses and fungi, living amid decomposing plants and various minerals.
items.explain: Q14: The passage says healthy soil contains *'various minerals'* alongside bacteria and decomposing plants. The question asks what else is in soil besides microorganisms and plant remains — **'minerals'** is the missing piece. So the answer is **minerals**.

items.sentence_raw: That means soils do not just grow our food, but are the source of nearly all our existing antibiotics, and could be our best hope in the fight against antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

Soil is also an ally against climate change: as microorganisms within soil digest dead animals and plants, they lock in their carbon content, holding three times the amount of carbon as does the entire atmosphere.
items.explain: Q15: The passage explains soil helps fight climate change because microorganisms *'lock in their carbon content'* — this means soil **stores** carbon. The question asks what soil stores that affects the climate, so the answer is **carbon**.

items.sentence_raw: Soils also store water, preventing flood damage: in the UK, damage to buildings, roads and bridges from floods caused by soil degradation costs £233 million every year.
items.explain: Q16: The passage says *'Soils also store water, preventing flood damage'* to buildings, roads and bridges. The question says soil prevents damage to property by holding something — that something is **water**.

items.sentence_raw: If the soil loses its ability to perform these functions, the human race could be in big trouble.
The danger is not that the soil will disappear completely, but that the microorganisms that give it its special properties will be lost.
And once this has happened, it may take the soil thousands of years to recover.
Agriculture is by far the biggest problem.
items.explain: Q17: The passage states *'Agriculture is by far the biggest problem'* for soil degradation. The question asks for the main factor causing soil degradation from human activity, so the answer is **agriculture**.

items.sentence_raw: In the wild, when plants grow they remove nutrients from the soil, but then when the plants die and decay these nutrients are returned directly to the soil.
items.explain: Q23: The passage explains *'In the wild, when plants grow they remove nutrients from the soil, but then when the plants die and decay these nutrients are returned directly to the soil'* — this shows how soil stayed healthy before farming. This is in section **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Humans tend not to return unused parts of harvested crops directly to the soil to enrich it, meaning that the soil gradually becomes less fertile.
items.explain: Q18: The passage says *'Humans tend not to return unused parts of harvested crops directly to the soil'* — this means nutrients in those unused parts **may not be put back into the soil**. So the correct ending is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: In the past we developed strategies to get around the problem, such as regularly varying the types of crops grown, or leaving fields uncultivated for a season.
But these practices became inconvenient as populations grew and agriculture had to be run on more commercial lines.
A solution came in the early 20th century with the Haber-Bosch process for manufacturing ammonium nitrate.
Farmers have been putting this synthetic fertiliser on their fields ever since.
But over the past few decades, it has become clear this wasn't such a bright idea.
Chemical fertilisers can release polluting nitrous oxide into the atmosphere and excess is often washed away with the rain, releasing nitrogen into rivers.
items.explain: Q19: The passage says chemical fertilisers *'release polluting nitrous oxide into the atmosphere'* and wash nitrogen into rivers — this means they **may cause damage to different aspects of the environment**. So the correct ending is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: More recently, we have found that indiscriminate use of fertilisers hurts the soil itself, turning it acidic and salty, and degrading the soil they are supposed to nourish.
One of the people looking for a solution to this problem is Pius Floris, who started out running a tree-care business in the Netherlands, and now advises some of the world's top soil scientists.
He came to realise that the best way to ensure his trees flourished was to take care of the soil, and has developed a cocktail of beneficial bacteria, fungi and humus* to do this.
items.explain: Q22: The passage says Pius Floris *'came to realise that the best way to ensure his trees flourished was to take care of the soil'* — this is his personal motivation for creating the soil-improvement mixture. This information is in section **E**.

items.sentence_raw: Researchers at the University of Valladolid in Spain recently used this cocktail on soils destroyed by years of fertiliser overuse.
When they applied Floris's mix to the desert-like test plots, a good crop of plants emerged that were not just healthy at the surface, but had roots strong enough to pierce dirt as hard as rock.
items.explain: Q20: The passage says when Floris's mix was applied, *'a good crop of plants emerged'* with strong roots — this means the mixture **may improve the number and quality of plants growing there**. So the correct ending is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: The few plants that grew in the control plots, fed with traditional fertilisers, were small and weak.
However, measures like this are not enough to solve the global soil degradation problem.
To assess our options on a global scale we first need an accurate picture of what types of soil are out there, and the problems they face.
That's not easy.
For one thing, there is no agreed international system for classifying soil.
items.explain: Q26: The passage says *'there is no agreed international system for classifying soil'* — this lack of a shared system makes it hard to get a clear overview of soil degradation. This is in section **F**.

items.sentence_raw: In an attempt to unify the different approaches, the UN has created the Global Soil Map project.

Researchers from nine countries are working together to create a map linked to a database that can be fed measurements from field surveys, drone surveys, satellite imagery, lab analyses and so on to provide real-time data on the state of the soil.
items.explain: Q24: The passage lists *'field surveys, drone surveys, satellite imagery, lab analyses and so on'* as different ways to collect data on soil — these are examples of collecting information on soil degradation. This is in section **F**.

items.sentence_raw: Within the next four years, they aim to have mapped soils worldwide to a depth of 100 metres, with the results freely accessible to all.
But this is only a first step.
We need ways of presenting the problem that bring it home to governments and the wider public, says Pamela Chasek at the International Institute for Sustainable Development, in Winnipeg, Canada.
"Most scientists don't speak language that policy-makers can understand, and vice versa."
Chasek and her colleagues have proposed a goal of 'zero net land degradation'.
Like the idea of carbon neutrality, it is an easily understood target that can help shape expectations and encourage action.
items.explain: Q21: The passage says 'zero net land degradation' is *'an easily understood target that can help shape expectations and encourage action'* — this means it **may help governments to be more aware of soil-related issues**. So the correct ending is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: For soils on the brink, that may be too late.
Several researchers are agitating for the immediate creation of protected zones for endangered soils.
items.explain: Q25: The passage mentions *'the immediate creation of protected zones for endangered soils'* — this is a suggestion for keeping some soils safe soon. This is in section **G**.

items.sentence_raw: One difficulty here is defining what these areas should conserve: areas where the greatest soil diversity is present?
Or areas of unspoilt soils that could act as a future benchmark of quality?
Whatever we do, if we want our soils to survive, we need to take action now.

items.sentence_raw: "Happiness is the ultimate goal because it is self-evidently good.
If we are asked why happiness matters we can give no further external reason.
It just obviously does matter."
This pronouncement by Richard Layard, an economist and advocate of 'positive psychology', summarises the beliefs of many people today.
For Layard and others like him, it is obvious that the purpose of government is to promote a state of collective well-being.

The only question is how to achieve it, and here positive psychology - a supposed science that not only identifies what makes people happy but also allows their happiness to be measured - can show the way.
Equipped with this science, they say, governments can secure happiness in society in a way they never could in the past.
It is an astonishingly crude and simple-minded way of thinking, and for that very reason increasingly popular.

Those who think in this way are oblivious to the vast philosophical literature in which the meaning and value of happiness have been explored and questioned, and write as if nothing of any importance had been thought on the subject until it came to their attention.
It was the philosopher Jeremy Bentham (1748-1832) who was more than anyone else responsible for the development of this way of thinking.
For Bentham it was obvious that the human good consists of pleasure and the absence of pain.

The Greek philosopher Aristotle may have identified happiness with self-realisation in the 4th century BC, and thinkers throughout the ages may have struggled to reconcile the pursuit of happiness with other human values, but for Bentham all this was mere metaphysics or fiction.
items.explain: Q28: The passage mentions Aristotle to show he had a different idea: he *'identified happiness with self-realisation'*, not just pleasure. This is used to contrast with Bentham's view that happiness is only *'pleasure and the absence of pain'*. So the reviewer uses Aristotle to suggest that happiness **may not be just pleasure and the absence of pain** — answer **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Without knowing anything much of him or the school of moral theory he established - since they are by education and intellectual conviction illiterate in the history of ideas - our advocates of positive psychology follow in his tracks in rejecting as outmoded and irrelevant pretty much the entirety of ethical reflection on human happiness to date.
items.explain: Q27: The passage says advocates of positive psychology are *'illiterate in the history of ideas'* and reject *'the entirety of ethical reflection on human happiness to date'*. This means they simply do not know about the important ideas they should be thinking about. So the reviewer's attitude is that **they are ignorant about the ideas they should be considering** — answer **D**.

items.sentence_raw: But as William Davies notes in his recent book "The Happiness Industry", the view that happiness is the only self-evident good is actually a way of limiting moral inquiry.
One of the virtues of this rich, lucid and arresting book is that it places the current cult of happiness in a well-defined historical framework.
Rightly, Davies begins his story with Bentham, noting that he was far more than a philosopher.
Davies writes, "Bentham's activities were those which we might now associate with a public sector management consultant".

In the 1790s, he wrote to the Home Office suggesting that the departments of government be linked together through a set of 'conversation tubes', and to the Bank of England with a design for a printing device that could produce unforgeable banknotes.
items.explain:
Q30: The passage says Bentham suggested *'conversation tubes'* to link government departments. **'Conversation'** is about talking, which is a form of **communication**. So the answer is **F**.

Q31: The passage says Bentham designed a printing device to make *'unforgeable banknotes'*. If banknotes cannot be forged, they are safe and have more **security**. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: He drew up plans for a 'frigidarium' to keep provisions such as meat, fish, fruit and vegetables fresh.
items.explain: Q32: The passage says Bentham planned a *'frigidarium'* to keep food *'fresh'*. Keeping food fresh means stopping it from going bad, which is **preservation**. So the answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: His celebrated design for a prison to be known as a 'Panopticon', in which prisoners would be kept in solitary confinement while being visible at all times to the guards, was very nearly adopted.
items.explain: Q33: The passage describes the Panopticon prison where prisoners were *'visible at all times to the guards'*. Being visible means they were under constant **observation**. So the answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: (Surprisingly, Davies does not discuss the fact that Bentham meant his Panopticon not just as a model prison but also as an instrument of control that could be applied to schools and factories.)
Bentham was also a pioneer of the 'science of happiness'.
If happiness is to be regarded as a science, it has to be measured, and Bentham suggested two ways in which this might be done.
items.explain: Q34: The passage says for happiness to be a science, *'it has to be measured'*, and Bentham suggested ways to do this. So he investigated possibilities for its **measurement** — answer **A**.

items.sentence_raw: Viewing happiness as a complex of pleasurable sensations, he suggested that it might be quantified by measuring the human pulse rate.
Alternatively, money could be used as the standard for quantification: if two different goods have the same price, it can be claimed that they produce the same quantity of pleasure in the consumer.
Bentham was more attracted by the latter measure.

By associating money so closely to inner experience, Davies writes, Bentham "set the stage for the entangling of psychological research and capitalism that would shape the business practices of the twentieth century".
items.explain: Q29: Davies says Bentham's idea of linking money to happiness *'set the stage for the entangling of psychological research and capitalism'*. **'Entangling'** means connecting two things together. So this idea was significant because **it established a connection between work and psychology** — answer **B**.

items.sentence_raw: "The Happiness Industry" describes how the project of a science of happiness has become integral to capitalism.
We learn much that is interesting about how economic problems are being redefined and treated as psychological maladies.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says the book shows how economic problems are treated as *'psychological maladies'* and how measuring feelings has *'informed management studies and advertising'*. This is a clear discussion of the link between psychology and economics. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: In addition, Davies shows how the belief that inner states of pleasure and displeasure can be objectively measured has informed management studies and advertising.
items.explain: Q35: The passage says the book shows how economic problems are treated as *'psychological maladies'* and how measuring feelings has *'informed management studies and advertising'*. This is a clear discussion of the link between psychology and economics. So the answer is **YES**.

items.sentence_raw: The tendency of thinkers such as J B Watson, the founder of behaviourism*, was that human beings could be shaped, or manipulated, by policymakers and managers.
Watson had no factual basis for his view of human action.
When he became president of the American Psychological Association in 1915, he 'had never even studied a single human being': his research had been confined to experiments on white rats.
items.explain: Q37: The passage says Watson *'had never even studied a single human being'* before 1915 — his research was only on *'white rats'*. So the statement that his ideas were supported by research on humans is directly contradicted. The answer is **NO**.

items.sentence_raw: Yet Watson's reductive model is now widely applied, with 'behaviour change' becoming the goal of governments: in Britain, a 'Behaviour Insights Team' has been established by the government to study how people can be encouraged, at minimum cost to the public purse, to live in what are considered to be socially desirable ways.

items.sentence_raw: But whatever its intellectual pedigree, the idea that governments should be responsible for promoting happiness is always a threat to human freedom.
